title: What can the sky tell us about economic recovery? The case of the West Bank & Gaza
gist: World Bank economists use Sentinel-5P NO₂ and nighttime-lights data to show that economic disruption in the West Bank and Gaza after October 2023 was deep, widespread and persistent, continuing past the October 2025 ceasefire. Gaza's 3.1% y/y Q1 2026 GDP growth is framed as a rebound from a depressed base, not recovery.

themes.theme: Satellite data as an economic monitor in conflict

insights.claim: Nighttime lights and satellite-measured nitrogen dioxide can complement conventional economic statistics, offering more timely and geographically detailed views of disruption, especially where conflict impedes data collection.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Alternative satellite data can nowcast activity in frontier or conflict economies where official data lag.

insights.claim: NO₂ is a short-lived pollutant produced mainly by fuel combustion from vehicles, power generation and industry, so changes in it provide an independent signal of combustion-intensive economic activity.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: NO₂ is a usable proxy for mobility and industrial output in alt-data models.

insights.claim: The authors used weekly NO₂ observations from the EU's Copernicus Sentinel-5P satellite, separated trend from seasonal and short-term noise, and compared the 52 weeks before and after October 2023.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: A replicable method for satellite-based activity tracking.

insights.claim: NO₂ levels in the year after October 2023 were nearly 10 percent lower in Gaza and around 2 percent lower in the West Bank than in the preceding year.

themes.theme: Limits and proper use of satellite indicators

insights.claim: NO₂ is not produced exclusively by economic activity, and weather, cloud cover, atmospheric chemistry, fires and changes in energy mix can all affect observed concentrations.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Alt-data users must control for non-economic noise in satellite pollution signals.

insights.claim: The authors argue satellite indicators should be treated as corroborating evidence for triangulation rather than an alternative set of national accounts, helping distinguish genuine recovery from statistical rebounds.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Satellite data are best used to test whether headline rebounds reflect real activity.
insights.quote: Satellite indicators should therefore be treated as corroborating evidence, not as an alternative set of national accounts.
